questions.q: Near a band edge, a band that is flat (has little curvature) means the carriers in it are…
options: Heavy: effective mass is inversely proportional to the band's curvature
Light: effective mass is proportional to the band's curvature
Unable to move at all, because a flat band has no available states
Exactly as heavy as a free electron, whatever the band's shape
questions.explain: Near a band edge the band is a parabola, and the carrier behaves like a particle with an effective mass m* that is inversely proportional to the curvature. A flat band means a heavy carrier.

questions.q: Why are holes in silicon slower than electrons?
options: The valence band is flatter, so holes have a heavier effective mass
Holes are disrupted by the broken bonds they leave behind as they move
There are far fewer holes than electrons in every piece of silicon
Holes carry a positive charge, so the electric field pushes them less
questions.explain: Holes are slower because the valence band is flatter, which means a heavier effective mass. Explanations about 'bond disruptions' are a common pitfall and do not survive scrutiny.

questions.q: Mobility is μ = qτ/m*. What are the only two ways to make carriers more mobile?
options: Make collisions rarer (longer τ) or make the carriers lighter (smaller m*)
Make collisions more frequent (shorter τ) or make the carriers heavier (larger m*)
Raise τ and m* together by the same factor
Make the electric field stronger or the channel longer
questions.explain: Mobility depends only on the mean time between collisions τ and the effective mass m*. Rare collisions and light carriers are the two levers; nothing else enters.

questions.q: The graph shows the mobility of electrons and holes in bulk silicon against doping. Why does mobility fall at high doping?
questions.alt: Bulk silicon mobility against total dopant concentration: electrons fall from about 1400 to under 100 cm²/V·s and holes from about 470 to about 50 as doping rises from 10¹⁶ to 10²⁰ cm⁻³
options: Carriers scatter off the many ionised dopant atoms, so collisions become more frequent
The extra dopant atoms make the carriers heavier, so they accelerate more slowly
Heavily doped silicon runs hotter, so the lattice vibrates harder
The band gap disappears at high doping, so the carriers can no longer move
questions.explain: At low doping, scattering by lattice vibrations (phonons) sets the mobility. At high doping, scattering by the charged, ionised dopant atoms takes over and mobility falls steeply.

questions.q: The graph shows drift velocity against electric field in silicon. Why does the velocity stop rising near 10⁷ cm/s?
questions.alt: Drift velocity against field on log scales: electrons and holes follow v = μE at low field, then level off near 10⁷ cm/s above about 10⁴ to 10⁵ V/cm
options: Fast carriers emit optical phonons, losing energy as fast as the field gives it to them
The carriers reach the speed of light inside silicon and cannot go any faster
The field pushes the carriers out of the channel into the gate oxide
At high field all the carriers turn into holes, which are slower than electrons
questions.explain: Once a carrier has enough energy to emit an optical phonon, energy is removed as fast as the field supplies it, and the velocity levels off at v_sat ≈ 10⁷ cm/s. A modern transistor works mostly in this regime.

questions.q: Why are a carrier's diffusion coefficient D and its mobility μ linked (the Einstein relation)?
options: Both are set by the same random collisions that carriers undergo
Both are set by the band gap, which fixes how many carriers there are
Both depend only on the gate voltage applied to the transistor
They are not linked: D and μ are measured separately and are unrelated
questions.explain: Drift and diffusion come from the same collisions, so D = μ·kT/q. At 300 K, kT/q = 25.9 mV. The relation holds for non-degenerate material.

questions.q: The picture shows the bands of a MOS capacitor in three regimes. In depletion (b), what is left near the silicon surface?
questions.alt: Band diagrams of a MOS capacitor on p-type silicon: (a) accumulation with holes at the surface, (b) depletion with bands bent down over a depletion width W, (c) inversion with a thin layer of electrons at the surface
options: Fixed negative acceptor ions: the holes have been pushed away from the surface
A thin sheet of free electrons that forms the conducting channel
A layer of extra holes that has been pulled up to the surface
Nothing at all: the surface region is completely empty of charge
questions.explain: In depletion the gate pushes the holes away, leaving the fixed, negatively charged acceptor ions behind. Only at higher gate voltage, in inversion (c), does a sheet of electrons form the channel.

questions.q: How do modern transistors mainly set their threshold voltage?
options: By choosing the work function of the metal gate
By making the gate oxide thicker or thinner
By heavily doping the channel under the gate
By heating the transistor to a set temperature
questions.explain: In older transistors V_T was set by channel doping. Modern devices, with undoped channels, set V_T by the work function of the metal gate.

questions.q: When the carriers in a channel travel at their saturation velocity, how does the drain current behave?
options: It rises in a straight line with gate overdrive and no longer depends on the channel length
It rises with the square of the gate overdrive and doubles every time the channel is halved
It falls as the gate voltage rises, because the carriers slow down at high field
It stays zero until the drain voltage exceeds the gate voltage
questions.explain: With velocity saturation, I_D ≈ W·C_ox·v_sat·(V_GS − V_T): linear in overdrive and independent of L. The long-channel square law overestimates the drive current of a modern transistor.

questions.q: The graph shows three transistors with the same threshold voltage but different subthreshold swings. Which one has the lowest off-current at V_GS = 0?
questions.alt: Drain current on a log scale against gate voltage for three transistors crossing at the same threshold: swings of 60, 75 and 95 mV per decade; at V_GS = 0 their off-currents differ by more than three decades
options: The one with the steepest curve, a swing of 60 mV per decade
The one with the flattest curve, a swing of 95 mV per decade
The one in the middle, a swing of 75 mV per decade
All three are the same, because they share the same threshold
questions.explain: Below threshold the current falls exponentially, by ten times for every 'swing' of gate voltage. The steeper the curve (the smaller the swing), the lower the current at V_GS = 0: here the off-currents differ by more than three decades.

questions.q: Electron mobility in bulk silicon reaches about 1400 cm²/V·s, but in a modern transistor's inversion layer it is only 200–400. What is the main reason?
options: The vertical field presses carriers against an interface that is not atomically flat, so they scatter off its roughness
The inversion layer contains many more dopant atoms than bulk silicon, so carriers scatter off them
Carriers in the inversion layer are heavier, because the gate's field adds to their mass
The wavefunction leaks into the oxide, where the electrons carry current very slowly
questions.explain: At high vertical field, carriers are pressed against the Si/oxide interface, which is not atomically flat: surface-roughness scattering. Charges and vibrations in the high-k dielectric add more. (The tail of the wavefunction in the oxide carries no current: a common pitfall.)

questions.q: Why is the drift-diffusion model only an approximation for today's transistors?
options: The gate length is now about the same as the mean free path, so carriers collide only once or twice on the way
The gate length is now about a hundred times the mean free path, so carriers collide too often to model
Today's transistors use holes instead of electrons, and drift-diffusion applies only to electrons
The supply voltage is now so low that no current flows by drift, only by diffusion
questions.explain: Drift-diffusion assumes many collisions in the channel. With a mean free path of about 10 nm and gate lengths of 12–20 nm, a carrier scatters only once or twice: transport is quasi-ballistic.
